The first sentence has two claimants. Wesley assigns it to the bridegroom, comparing himself to rose and lily for fragrance and beauty. Henry hears the same voice and finds condescension in it, the Son of the Highest owning himself a flower of the field to show how easy the access is, and preferring the lily's clothing to Solomon's glory. The others give it to the bride. Clarke makes it modesty answering a compliment: called fair, she returns that she is only a common flower of the field, which he denies at once by setting the lily against the bramble. Delitzsch presses the grammar the same way: she claims to be not the meadow-flower but one of the class, the article belonging only to the second half of the phrase. Ellicott hears a snatch of song after the eulogies, and says the claim is nothing like a queen lily and rose in one. Gill reports the Jewish writers taking it of the church and inclines with them.

Which flower it is nobody settles. Ellicott works from the derivation, which points to a bulb, and finds the sweet-scented narcissus best; the crocus has been suggested but has no perfume, and no bulb is more fragrant, the East loving it so well that in season it fills the bazaars and men as well as women carry blossoms and keep smelling them. Another prefers the mallow on its Arabic name, and in the only other place the word occurs the old versions render it lily, many moderns the autumn crocus. Delitzsch takes the Syriac reading and gets the meadow saffron, the flesh-coloured flower on a leafless stem that decks mown fields by thousands, and passes on its name, son before father, the blossom coming up before the leaves.

The answer turns the modesty into a compliment. Gill observes that the comparison is not about where lilies grow but what they are worth beside thorns, and credits an earlier commentator with seeing that the second half proves it, setting her against the other maidens rather than among them. He fills the thorns with content: men unprofitable and hurtful and destined for burning, persecutors above all, whose neighbourhood sets off what stands among them. Ellicott glosses in four words: the daughters are the other maidens.

She answers with a tree, and Ellicott turns botanist. Four things are required of it across the book: grateful shade, agreeable taste, sweet perfume, a golden look. The apple he sets aside, what Palestine calls an apple being really a quince and the climate too hot for ours. The quince fails on taste, being astringent until cooked, though the ancients had consecrated it to love. The citron is disputed, one denying it shade and another calling it large and beautiful with deep shade and golden fruit. The apricot meets every requirement and is, after the fig, the most abundant fruit in the country. Clarke goes no further than apple or citron. Delitzsch derives the name from a root for breathing and makes the tree king among fruit trees, the forest word meaning rough and rugged ground where trees bear mostly sour fruit.

The shade and the fruit are read as one experience. Delitzsch notes the wood has fruit trees too, but unpalatable ones, where this joins delicious fruit to grateful shade, and that the Hebrew says more than that she wanted to sit down, the wanting completing itself in the sitting. Henry takes the benefits separately: shade for a soul parched with conviction or fatigued with the world, as when a prophet sat under a juniper; then the fruit, sweet to one who has tried it. Clarke compresses the verse into a sentence about union and a happiness he cannot describe. Gill runs the comparison up the ranks, angels who are sons by creation and princes who are lofty trees, setting the beloved above either.
4:
What the house of wine is depends on how literally it is read. Clarke takes it literally: the ancients kept wine not in cellars but in large jars along the wall of an upper room, where the most precious things were stored, and prints a passage of Homer to show it, the lofty chamber with brass and gold, chests of garments, jars of oil, rows of old wine against the wall. Gill hesitates between store-room and feast, settles on a banqueting house, and reads the gospel feast to which the King of kings leads his people by the hand. Delitzsch rules out the vineyard, which would be named differently, and puts her in the chamber where the king entertains his friends, a sunburnt girl who does not belong there, covered by a banner that shields her shame. Ellicott refuses all three: it is simply the place of the delights of love.

Then the flagons, which are probably not flagons. Ellicott reports a dried cake of uncertain material, possibly of grapes, among the gifts distributed at the ark's removal and rendered there as something from the frying-pan, while here the Greek gives sweet unguents and the Latin flowers; the English follows a rabbinic reading. Delitzsch settles on grape-cakes, distinct from dried grapes and fig-cakes, and rejects the quinces and citrons others propose for the apples, which here refresh rather than symbolise. On the second verb Ellicott notes the margin would strew her with apples, so some make a bed of apple-leaves, but the parallel word is against it, both meaning to prop underneath. Clarke tells of a preacher who took the verse for his text, repeated it, was overwhelmed and could not go on; he allows the sincerity but questions the judgment.

The embrace is followed by a warning, disputed twice over. Gill weighs whether church or Christ speaks and finds reasons both ways: the address is to the virgins and the manner adjuration, yet it was the church who lay in the arms. Ellicott settles it against the received text on grammar: the words mean till she please, not till he, the poet imagining his beloved asleep and playfully telling her companions not to intrude. Delitzsch reads the same and pauses on the oath, since Israelites may swear only by God, though adjuring by what is not God is allowed, perhaps the only direct instance in Scripture.

The second movement opens with a sound. Henry has her know the voice before she sees the speaker, as a sheep does, and finds triumph in the claim that no other voice can speak to the heart and make it burn. Delitzsch treats the word for voice as an interjection, hark rather than a noun, and works the two verbs of springing, the second meaning to gather for a leap. Ellicott finds no need of the clumsy device that puts the heroine in a dream, taking the passage for a remembered morning put into her mouth, and quotes Tennyson on knowing the beloved comes before he mounts the hill.

The last posture is what the allegorists could not leave alone. Clarke keeps to the architecture: the wall enclosed a court, and he was seen behind it, then within, then at the window. Delitzsch keeps the gazelle in view, bounding up and then peering. Ellicott, as a specimen of what allegory can do with one clause, sets out five readings of that wall: our mortal condition; the middle wall of partition, the law; the iniquities that keep a voice from reaching us; the creatures behind whom God stands and through whom he speaks; and, if it may be said, the flesh of Christ spread over his divinity, through which it sounds sweetly and alters its voice. He returns to the verb, whose root idea is looking bright, the beloved making his eyes glance through the lattice.
10:
Before the spring song can be read, its status must be fixed. Delitzsch rules out a dream on the plainest ground, that she does not call it one; the scene is dramatic only at second hand, since she speaks in monologue, narrating something that happened between the courtship's beginning and her coming home. He turns on a scholar who filled the poem out with such formulas till it became a chain of narrative declaimed to the daughters, objecting that this stops it being dramatic and makes it tedious with its interposed he said and I said.

The winter divides them. Clarke, following travellers, reports that at Aleppo one part of the cold season is marked off for its severity, lasts about forty days, and has its own name; he proposes the Hebrew word here for that, since it occurs nowhere else and another word covers the rainy season. The gain is that the second clause then adds something. Ellicott takes the same rare word from a root meaning to overcast and gets the season of cloud and gloom, noting that Wordsworth used the line of an early spring in a very different climate. Delitzsch derives it from concealing or veiling, and observes that in the East winter simply is the rainy season, the common word for rain in Jerusalem today being that word.

Then the season's noises. Ellicott concedes the word may mean pruning, as the old versions took it, but holds the parallel requires singing, and defends the supplied birds: the context means the untaught harmony of spring rather than voices of men, though he admits no authority beyond the context and that scriptural allusions to birdsong are very few. On the figs Ellicott renders that the tree has ripened its unripe fruit, not the early crop that comes before the leaves but the green fruit that hung through winter. Gill objects to the usual translation because the fig puts out fruit at once and does not blossom, and reports a Jewish reading making the word mean the sweetening. Clarke, who never saw a healthy fig tree naked, has it bearing all year where climate allows.

The dove is a compliment about temperament. Ellicott identifies the rock pigeon, which chooses lofty cliffs and deep ravines and avoids men, so the poet prettily indicates his beloved's shyness. Henry keeps the bird and moralises it: beauty, innocence, quietness, faithful as the turtle to her mate, the dove that descended on Christ descending on Christians to make them meek. On the foxes, Gill cannot decide whether Christ or the church gives the order and suspects both together; Delitzsch makes it a little song of her own, a vine-dresser's ditty natural to a girl who had kept a vineyard; Clarke gives it to the bridegroom instructing his companions. Ellicott places it in a genre, the poet's traditional warning-off of troublesome creatures, as Spenser banishes owls and ravens and frogs from a wedding night and Theocritus curses the brush-tailed foxes that spoil a neighbour's vines; the allegorists, he adds, make them heretics.

The last verse cannot even be dated to a time of day. Clarke reads dawn, since the word means to breathe and first light comes with refreshing breezes, and takes the fleeing shadows for sunset, when shadows vanish. Ellicott reads the same verb as cooling and gets evening, when the breeze sets in, holding the point fixed by shadows that flee by lengthening rather than vanishing; he supports it from Virgil and from Tennyson on shadows three times as long as before. Delitzsch keeps the sense of before evening, so what she asks may be done first. On the place-name Clarke offers mountains of division and guesses a site beyond Jordan named for a partition; Ellicott reports the Greek reading of ravines, and cannot choose whether the hills divide the lovers or are cut by valleys.
